page.title: Welcome
page.heading: {{moduleTitle}}
page.content:
Welcome to {{moduleTitle}}.

In this course you will learn to prepare for the field, separate facts from opinions, cite specifications and drawings precisely, write issues using "Not IAW" and "Contrary to", create and cross-reference issues, define clear solutions, and stay factual when the conversation gets heated.

The GC and subs can argue with an opinion. They cannot argue with a fact.

block.grid.cmp.text: Before stepping onto a job site, it is critical to establish the right foundational mindset and complete essential preparatory steps. Commissioning is not just an isolated task or a simple box to check; it is a collaborative, team-based process that requires asking data-backed questions. Ultimately, effective commissioning serves to connect different disciplines, protect the overall project vision, validate the design, and ensure both building function and accountability.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Pre-Inspection Preparation
cmp.stack.cmp.text: To ensure a successful and efficient site visit, field agents must complete thorough pre-inspection groundwork. Proper preparation prevents delays and ensures that you are operating with the most up-to-date information.

block.grid.cmp.text: In the field, you will rely on specific software tools to manage your inspections, execute initial checks, and track issues. Understanding the distinct roles of these platforms—and the strict rules for using them—is crucial for maintaining accurate project records and ensuring quality control.

Our value in the field comes from one thing: credibility. Every time we raise an issue, the General Contractor and subcontractors decide whether to act on it. An opinion invites a debate. A fact backed by the contract documents ends one.

The GC and subs can argue with an opinion. They cannot argue with a fact.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: What Counts as a Fact?
cmp.stack.cmp.text: In commissioning, a fact is an observed, verifiable condition that you can compare against a written requirement. Before you raise anything as a deficiency, put it through the three-question Fact Test:

block.grid.cmp.text: If the answer to all three is yes, you have a fact-based issue. If the answer to question 1 is no, you have an opinion. It may still be a good one, but it is not a contract deficiency, and it must not be presented as one.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Opinion vs. Fact: Side by Side
cmp.stack.cmp.text:
The same field observation can be stated as an opinion or as a fact. Notice that the fact-based version names the location, describes the condition objectively, and cites the requirement.

Note: Section, article, paragraph, sheet and detail numbers in this course are illustrative examples. Always cite from your own project's current documents.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Where Opinions Belong
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Experience matters. Your opinion, based on years in the field, is often right, and the owner may want to hear it. But it must be labeled honestly and routed to the right people:

block.grid.cmp.text:
• Deficiency / Issue: does not meet a written requirement. Assigned to the responsible contractor. Must include a citation.
  • Observation: a condition worth tracking that you cannot yet tie to a requirement, or cannot yet verify. Stated neutrally, without assigning fault.
  • Recommendation: your professional opinion or a best practice that goes beyond the contract documents. Routed to the owner and design team for a decision, not assigned to the contractor as a deficiency.

Use a clear label so no one confuses the two, for example: "Recommendation (not a contract requirement): Consider adding isolation valves at each VAV reheat coil to simplify future maintenance. Owner and EOR to decide."

Presenting an opinion as a requirement is the fastest way to lose credibility. Once a contractor catches one unsupported "requirement," they will question every issue you write after it.

A fact-based issue is only as strong as its citation. "Per spec" or "per code" is not a citation. It sends the contractor on a scavenger hunt and signals that you may not have looked it up yourself. A proper citation points to the exact sentence that governs the condition.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Know Where Requirements Live
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Requirements come from several sources. Know them, and know which one governs:

block.grid.cmp.text:
• Specifications: the written requirements, organized by CSI MasterFormat division and section.
  • Drawings: plans, sections, details, schedules, keynotes and general notes.
  • Addenda, ASIs, Bulletins and Change Orders: these modify the original documents. A requirement you cite may have been changed.
  • RFI Responses: the design team's clarifications. Check for one before you write an issue on a condition that might have already been answered.
  • Approved Submittals: what the contractor committed to install, including approved deviations.
  • Manufacturer Installation Instructions (IOMs): usually made enforceable by the spec (e.g., "install in accordance with manufacturer's written instructions"). Cite both.
  • Owner's Project Requirements (OPR), Basis of Design (BOD) and Owner Design Standards: the owner's intent and program standards.
  • Referenced Codes and Standards: cite the edition adopted by the Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) or referenced in the spec, not simply the newest edition.
When documents conflict, the project's order of precedence clause (typically in the General Conditions or Division 01) decides which one governs. Read it on every project. Do not assume.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Anatomy of a Spec Citation
cmp.stack.cmp.text:
Specifications follow a consistent structure. Learn to read it so you can cite down to the paragraph:

Written out, that is: Spec 23 07 13, 3.2.A.1. Most field installation issues will be found in Part 3 – Execution.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Weak vs. Strong Citations
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Note: Section, article, paragraph, sheet and detail numbers in this course are illustrative examples. Always cite from your own project's current documents.

page.title: Writing the Issue Statement: Not IAW / Contrary To

block.grid.cmp.text: Every issue should be written so that someone who has never been to the site can read it, find the location, understand exactly what is wrong, see the requirement it violates, and know what "fixed" looks like. The standard phrasing we use to tie a condition to a requirement is Not IAW (Not In Accordance With) or Contrary to.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: The Issue Formula
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Build every issue statement from the same five parts, in the same order:

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Choosing the Right Phrase
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Note: Section, article, paragraph, sheet and detail numbers in this course are illustrative examples. Always cite from your own project's current documents.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Putting It Together
cmp.stack.cmp.text:
Before (opinion-based):

"Sensor missing on VAV. Needs to be fixed ASAP."

After (fact-based):

"Level 2, Room 214, VAV-2-14: Discharge air temperature sensor not installed. Not IAW Spec 23 09 23, 3.4.C: 'Provide discharge air temperature sensor at each VAV box with reheat.' Required action: Install DAT sensor per Spec 23 09 23 and approved submittal 23 09 23-004, verify point reads correctly at the BAS front end, and notify CxA for re-inspection. See Photos 1–2."

The second version can be assigned, priced, fixed and closed without a single phone call. That is the goal.

block.grid.cmp.text:
• Describe the condition, not the person. No blame, sarcasm or judgment.
  • Use numbers and units. "Measured 30 in." beats "too close." "Reading 58°F vs. 55°F setpoint" beats "running warm."
  • One deficiency per issue. If the same deficiency occurs at multiple identical locations, list each location (or follow the project's systemic-issue convention).
  • Avoid absolutes and emotion. No "never," "always," "terrible," ALL CAPS or exclamation points.
  • Use tags exactly as they appear on the drawings and equipment schedules. So the issue can be searched, sorted and found.
  • Read it back. Before saving, ask: could someone who was not with me find this, understand it and fix it?

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Required Elements of Every Issue
cmp.stack.cmp.text: When you identify a problem in the field, creating a rigorous and detailed record is essential. A standard issue requires a precise, non-generic description and must be assigned to the appropriate responsible party or the General Contractor. You must also identify the root cause based on evidence and set a realistic due date that aligns with the quality specifications. To guarantee zero ambiguity, every issue must be directly anchored to the design documents. This means referencing exact specification sections, such as 23 09 23.14, and including specific drawing sheet numbers, like M-102, to pinpoint the exact location. Visual evidence is equally important. When standardizing your photo-documentation, always follow a four-step process: capture a wide context shot to show the location, take a close-up detail shot to clearly show the problem, ensure proper lighting, and add clear, descriptive markups to highlight the exact area of concern

block.grid.cmp.text: A well-written issue that cannot be found, or that duplicates three others, still slows the project down. How you create and connect issues in the issues platform (e.g., Cx Alloy) matters as much as how you write them.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Before You Create: Search First
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Before logging a new issue, search the platform for the equipment tag and location. Ask:

block.grid.cmp.text:
• Is this condition already logged as an open issue? If so, add your new photos and comments to the existing issue instead of creating a duplicate.
  • Was this issue previously closed? If the condition has come back, create a new issue that references the closed one (see below).
  • Is there an RFI, ASI or approved deviation that already addresses this condition?

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Complete Every Field
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Every issue should include, at minimum:

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Referencing Other Issues and Documents
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Use consistent language to tie issues together so the history is clear:

block.grid.cmp.text:
• Add updates as new, dated comments. Do not overwrite the original description in a way that changes its meaning.
  • Never close an issue without verification (re-inspection, Delta Walk or retest).
  • When a contractor provides a document that resolves the issue (e.g., an RFI response or approved deviation), cite it in the closing comment.
An issue without a path to closure is just a complaint. Every issue we write must answer the contractor's next question: "What do you need me to do to close this?"

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: State What Compliance Looks Like
cmp.stack.cmp.text:
The required action should describe the end condition that satisfies the cited requirement, and how it will be verified. For example:

"Install duct insulation on AHU-2 discharge duct per Spec 23 07 13, 3.2.A. Notify CxA when complete for re-inspection."

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Stay in Your Lane: What vs. How
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Our role is to define what compliance looks like, based on the documents. How the contractor achieves it (means and methods) is their responsibility, unless the documents specify the method. Telling a contractor how to do their work can shift responsibility onto us and the owner.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: When the Documents Are Unclear, Conflicting or Silent
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Do not fill the gap with your opinion. Instead:

block.grid.cmp.text:
• Unclear or conflicting: Log the issue and recommend clarification. "Drawing M-201 and Spec 23 36 00, 3.2.A conflict on VAV box access clearance. Recommend GC submit RFI to the EOR for clarification."
  • Silent: If no document addresses the condition, it is not a contract deficiency. Log it as an Observation or Recommendation for the owner and design team.
  • Different, but arguably better: It is still a deviation. Only the owner and EOR can accept a deviation. Route it to them; do not approve it in the field.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Weak vs. Strong Solutions
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Note: Section, article, paragraph, sheet and detail numbers in this course are illustrative examples. Always cite from your own project's current documents.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Define the Closure Criteria
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Say up front what evidence will close the issue, so there is no debate later: a re-inspection photo, a retest of specific functional test steps, a revised submittal, a test report, or a BAS trend. Match the closure criteria to the issue's priority (see Issue Classification).

page.title: Issue Classification and the Resolution Lifecycle

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Priority Levels and Closure
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Every issue you document must be classified accurately according to specification 01 40 00. A P0, or Critical, issue impacts system operation, facility readiness, or causes an immediate safety risk. It requires a response within 24 hours, a resolution within 3 days, a full system retest, and strictly halts equipment shipment from the integrator. A P1, or High, issue has a significant impact but poses no immediate safety threat. It requires a 48-hour response, a 7-day resolution, and a retest of only the failed steps. P2, or Medium, issues are not immediately critical but require the system to operate safely before moving on. They target a 14-day resolution, require visual inspection or a partial retest, and need formal owner approval to ship equipment. Finally, P3, or Low, issues are cosmetic or housekeeping in nature; they target a 30-day resolution, require only a visual inspection, and also need formal owner approval to ship. Once an issue is logged, you must track its lifecycle from 'Open' to 'Resolved' and finally to 'Closed'. As the commissioning agent, you are responsible for verifying the fix by conducting a re-inspection, known as a "Delta Walk," before updating the documentation to reflect a closed status.

block.grid.cmp.text:
Projects are moving at an unprecedented pace. That pace is exactly when shortcuts happen and credibility is lost. Speed does not excuse an unsupported call. A wrong issue logged in a hurry costs more time than it saves, and it weakens every issue you write after it.

Get back to the basics: be prepared before you walk, and be sure before you write.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Before the Walk: Pack Your References
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Have the documents in your hand, not back at the trailer. Mechanical rooms, basements and rooftops often have no signal, so download for offline use.

block.grid.cmp.text:
• Current spec sections for the systems you are inspecting (including Division 01: 01 40 00 and 01 91 00)
  • Current drawing sheets, including details, schedules and the latest revisions
  • Addenda, ASIs, bulletins and RFI responses that affect the area
  • Approved submittals and manufacturer IOMs for the equipment
  • The checklists or functional test scripts you will be executing
  • Open issues for the area and equipment, so you can verify and update them
  • Charged tablet with offline access, plus camera, flashlight and tape measure

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: In the Field: Slow Down to Be Right
cmp.stack.cmp.text: When you see something that looks wrong, run through this before you raise it:

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: "Let Me Verify That" Is a Professional Answer
cmp.stack.cmp.text:
If a contractor asks you to justify something and you do not have the reference in front of you, do not guess and do not argue. Say:

"Good question. Let me pull up the requirement and I'll follow up with the exact reference."

Then follow up. Every time. An issue logged an hour later with the right citation is worth far more than one logged right away on a hunch.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Field Readiness Checklist
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Before every site walk, confirm:

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Let the Documents Do the Talking
cmp.stack.cmp.text: During your inspections, you may occasionally face pushback or disagreements from contractors. When this happens, always base your requests on official client specifications and program design standards rather than relying on unwritten historical practices or "tribal knowledge". If a conflict or scope gap arises on site, you should immediately define and propose a practical solution, fostering open and collaborative teamwork. When referencing requirements to resolve disputes, point directly to Spec Section 01 40 00 for Quality Requirements and 01 91 00 for General Commissioning, which clearly define the required roles and procedures for all partners. Ultimately, this rigorous approach to documentation does more than just solve problems; it provides a clear record of quality and compliance, protects the overall integrity of the project, and builds lasting trust with both clients and contractors.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: When a Contractor Pushes Back
cmp.stack.cmp.text: Disagreements are normal. Arguments are optional. Keep the conversation on the documents:

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Words That Keep It Factual

block.grid.cmp.text:
Each scenario below starts with an issue written the way we too often see it in the field. Before reading the improved version, try rewriting it yourself using the issue formula: Location → Condition → Not IAW / Contrary to → Required Action → Evidence.

Note: Section, article, paragraph, sheet and detail numbers in this course are illustrative examples. Always cite from your own project's current documents.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Scenario 1: Insulation
cmp.stack.cmp.text:
As written: "Insulation is garbage on AHU-2. Sub needs to redo."

Rewritten: "AHU-2 – Discharge duct insulation incomplete. Level 3 mech room: approx. 6 ft of supply duct downstream of the AHU-2 discharge plenum is uninsulated. Not IAW Spec 23 07 13, 3.2.A. Required action: Insulate per Spec 23 07 13 and notify CxA for re-inspection. See Photos 1–2."

Why it works: It removes the judgment ("garbage"), states the actual condition and quantity, cites the requirement, and defines closure.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Scenario 2: Tribal Knowledge
cmp.stack.cmp.text:
As written: "We always put a strainer before the control valve. Add one."

Rewritten: "AHU-1 – Strainer missing upstream of CHW control valve CV-4. Contrary to Drawing M-501, Detail 3 (Rev 2), which shows a strainer with blow-down valve upstream of each coil control valve. Required action: Provide strainer per the cited detail. See Photo 3."

Why it works: "We always" is tribal knowledge. The drawing detail is a requirement. If the detail did not show a strainer, this would be a Recommendation to the owner and EOR, not a deficiency.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Scenario 3: The Contractor Pushes Back
cmp.stack.cmp.text:
Situation: You log that the flexible duct to VAV-2-14 is 9 ft long. The mechanical foreman says, "The engineer told us that was fine."

Opinion-based response: "Nobody runs flex that long. It's wrong."

Fact-based response: "Spec 23 33 00, 3.5.B limits flex runs to 5 ft. If there's an RFI response or approved deviation that allows the longer run, send me the number and I'll reference it and close the issue. Otherwise it stays open as written."

Why it works: It points to the document, invites the contractor to bring their own document, and keeps the conversation about facts. Facts work both ways: if they produce the RFI, close the issue gracefully and cite it.

cmp.stack.cmp.heading: Scenario 4: Can't Find the Requirement
cmp.stack.cmp.text:
Situation: A sensor is mounted in a spot you believe will give poor readings, but you cannot find a spec paragraph or detail that addresses its location.

Wrong move: Logging "Sensor in wrong location, relocate" as a deficiency assigned to the controls contractor.

Right move: Log a labeled Recommendation: "Recommendation (not a contract requirement): Duct static pressure sensor for AHU-3 is located approx. 2 ft downstream of a fitting, which may produce unstable readings. Owner and EOR to review whether relocation is desired."

Why it works: Your expertise is shared honestly, without presenting an opinion as a contract requirement.

block.grid.cmp.text: We need to get back to the basics and always be prepared in the field. Keep these principles with you on every walk.

block.grid.cmp.heading: The Six Elements of Every Issue

block.grid.cmp.text:
• Facts, not opinions. If you cannot cite it, it is not a deficiency.
  • Label opinions honestly as Observations or Recommendations, and route them to the owner and EOR.
  • Search before you create. Reference related, repeat and duplicate issues by number.
  • Define what compliance looks like, not how to build it.
  • When documents are unclear or conflicting, recommend an RFI. Do not fill the gap with opinion.
  • Bring your references. Don't rush. "Let me verify that" is a professional answer.
  • Facts work both ways. When a contractor shows a document that resolves the issue, cite it and close it.
The GC and subs can argue with an opinion. They cannot argue with a fact.

item.title: New list item
item.content: Commissioning brings clarity, alignment, and lasting performance.

item.title: Item title
item.content: It connects every discipline to protect the vision, validate design, and ensure accountability.

item.title: Item title
item.content: It is a team sport requiring collaboration and data-backed questions.

item.title: Item title
item.content: It is a deliberate, thoughtful, and collaborative process to ensure buildings function as intended.

item.title: Item title
item.content: Review Equipment Submittals: Take the time to thoroughly study and understand the specific materials and equipment that are being installed on the site.

item.title: Item title
item.content: Master the Sequences of Operation: Familiarize yourself with exactly how the systems are designed and intended to function in real-world scenarios.

item.title: Item title
item.content: Prepare Your Digital Tools: Gather all necessary reference drawings ahead of time and proactively verify your login access to required field platforms, such as BIM360 and Cx Alloy.

item.title: Item title
item.content: Ensure Mobile Readiness: Equip your tablet with mobile access to all project specifications, submittals, and drawings. Having these integrated platforms readily available in the palm of your hand prevents on-site delays and guarantees your inspections are perfectly aligned with the latest designs.

item.title: Item title
item.content: Check for Changes: Review addenda, ASIs, bulletins, RFI responses and open issues for the areas you will walk, so you are citing the current requirement.

item.title: Item 1
item.content: Can I cite it? Can I point to the specific document, section and paragraph (or sheet and detail) that requires something different?

item.title: Item 2
item.content: Can I show it? Do I have objective evidence, such as a photo, measurement, nameplate, reading or trend, that shows the condition?

item.title: Item 3
item.content: Would anyone reach the same conclusion? If another commissioning agent read the same paragraph and looked at the same condition, would they agree it does not comply?

item.title: Item 1
item.content: Quote the requirement. Include the key sentence in quotation marks so the reader does not have to look it up to understand the issue.

item.title: Item 2
item.content: Include the revision. Cite the current sheet revision or addendum. Citing a superseded document undermines the whole issue.

item.title: Item 3
item.content: Check for changes. Before citing, confirm no RFI, ASI, bulletin or approved deviation has modified the requirement.

item.title: Item 4
item.content: Cite the most specific source. If a detail on the drawing and a general spec paragraph both apply, cite both, starting with the most specific.

item.title: Item 5
item.content: If you cannot find it, say so. If you believe something is wrong but cannot find the requirement, log it as an Observation or ask the design team. Do not invent a requirement.

item.title: Item 1
item.content: Location and Equipment: building, level, room or gridline, and equipment tag. "Level 2, Room 214, VAV-2-14"

item.title: Item 2
item.content: Observed Condition: what you saw or measured, objectively, with units. "Discharge air temperature sensor not installed."

item.title: Item 3
item.content: Requirement: Not IAW / Contrary to the specific citation, with the key language quoted. "Not IAW Spec 23 09 23, 3.4.C: 'Provide discharge air temperature sensor at each VAV box with reheat.'"

item.title: Item 4
item.content: Required Action: what condition will bring it into compliance. "Install DAT sensor per the cited paragraph and the approved controls submittal."

item.title: Item 5
item.content: Evidence: attached photos (wide and close-up), readings or screenshots. "See Photos 1–2."

item.title: Item 1
item.content: Pause. Do not call it out on the spot just because it looks wrong.

item.title: Item 2
item.content: Find the requirement. Open the spec or drawing and read the actual paragraph.

item.title: Item 3
item.content: Confirm it is current. Check the revision, and check for an RFI, ASI or approved deviation that changed it.

item.title: Item 4
item.content: Verify the condition. Confirm the tag and location, measure it, and photograph it (wide and close-up).

item.title: Item 5
item.content: Then write it. Use the issue formula: location, condition, Not IAW / Contrary to, required action, evidence.

item.title: Item 1
item.content: I have the current specs, drawings and revisions for today's scope available offline.

item.title: Item 2
item.content: I have the approved submittals and IOMs for the equipment I'm inspecting.

item.title: Item 3
item.content: I have checked for RFIs, ASIs and bulletins that affect today's scope.

item.title: Item 4
item.content: I have reviewed the open issues for the areas I'm walking.

item.title: Item 5
item.content: My tablet is charged, and my platform logins (BIM360, Cx Alloy) work.

item.title: Item 6
item.content: I will cite before I call, and I will not rush an issue I cannot support.

item.title: Item 1
item.content: Location: building, level, room or gridline, and equipment tag

item.title: Item 2
item.content: Condition: what you observed or measured, objectively, with units

item.title: Item 3
item.content: Citation: Not IAW / Contrary to the specific section, paragraph, sheet or detail, with key language quoted

item.title: Item 4
item.content: Evidence: wide and close-up photos with markups, readings, screenshots

item.title: Item 5
item.content: Solution: the compliant end condition and how closure will be verified

item.title: Item 6
item.content: Classification: P0–P3 per Spec 01 40 00, with a realistic due date

item.title: Item 1
item.content: Listen and acknowledge. Let them make their case without interrupting.

item.title: Item 2
item.content: Open the document together. Pull up the cited paragraph or detail on your tablet and read it with them.

item.title: Item 3
item.content: Ask for their reference. If they believe the work is compliant, ask which document supports it (RFI response, ASI, approved submittal or deviation).

item.title: Item 4
item.content: Facts work both ways. If their document supersedes yours, accept it, cite it in the issue, and close or revise the issue.

item.title: Item 5
item.content: If it is genuinely unclear, stop debating. Recommend an RFI to the design team and note it in the issue.

item.title: Item 6
item.content: Escalate through the right channel. Unresolved disputes go to your Cx lead and the owner's representative, not into a field argument.

item.title: Item 7
item.content: Document the conversation. Add a dated comment to the issue summarizing what was discussed and the next step.
